gas-tx-caption: How gas moves in a message call, drawn as a fuel rig: the sender's pump fills a tank to the gas limit, the contract's engine uses what its code needs, and unused gas flows back through a meter.
gas-tx-description: A transaction enters the world state. Its sender reserves a gas supply equal to the transaction's gas limit. A message carries the call to the contract, whose EVM code runs and uses gas for each operation. When execution finishes, the unused gas, which is the gas limit minus the gas used, is returned to the sender. If execution runs out of gas, all of the gas supply is consumed, the contract's state changes are reverted, and nothing is returned.
diagram-readout-label: Gas for this scenario, in gas units
gas-tx-step-idle: Choose a scenario and send the transaction to follow its gas step by step.
gas-tx-step-enter: Step {step}: the transaction enters the world state with a gas limit of {limit} gas.
gas-tx-step-reserve: Step {step}: the sender reserves the full {limit} gas as the gas supply.
gas-tx-step-execute: Step {step}: the message reaches the contract, and its EVM code runs and uses {used} gas.
gas-tx-step-execute-out-of-gas: Step {step}: the EVM code needs more than {limit} gas, so it runs out of gas, uses all {limit} and fails.
gas-tx-step-return: Step {step}: the {returned} unused gas is returned to the sender.
gas-tx-step-revert: Step {step}: the contract's state changes are reverted, and no gas is returned.
gas-tx-definition-deck: The state of every account: balances, nonces, code and storage.
gas-tx-definition-order: The signed transaction. It sets the gas limit the call may spend.
gas-tx-definition-pump: The sender: the externally owned account that sends the transaction, pays for gas and gets unused gas back.
gas-tx-definition-tank: The gas supply: the gas limit, reserved before the code runs and drained as gas is used.
gas-tx-definition-feed: The message call, carried from the sender to the contract.
gas-tx-definition-engine: The contract: an account controlled by its EVM code, which uses gas for every operation it runs.
gas-tx-definition-return-line: Gas the call didn't use, flowing back to the sender.
gas-tx-definition-meter: How much unused gas is returned to the sender.
gas-evm-caption: Where gas goes inside the EVM: the transaction first pays a base intrinsic cost, then every operation draws its own cost from the gas supply. Stack and memory work is cheap; writing to storage costs the most.
gas-evm-description: A gas supply feeds the EVM through a pipe. Before any code runs, the transaction pays the base intrinsic cost of {intrinsic} gas. Then the program counter steps through seven opcodes: two PUSH1 put {value} and {slot} on the stack, MSTORE writes {value} to memory, two more PUSH1, then SSTORE writes {value} to a new storage slot, and STOP ends the run. Each opcode draws its cost from the supply; SSTORE alone costs {sstore} gas. With too little gas, execution runs out at SSTORE: all the gas is consumed and the write is reverted.
gas-evm-step-idle: Choose a scenario, then step through the code or run it.
gas-evm-step-intrinsic: Step {step}: before any code runs, the transaction pays the base intrinsic cost of {intrinsic} gas.
gas-evm-step-push1: PUSH1 puts {value} on the stack: {cost} gas.
gas-evm-step-mstore: MSTORE writes {value} to memory, growing it by one word: {cost} gas.
gas-evm-step-sstore: SSTORE writes {value} to a new storage slot, the most expensive kind of write: {cost} gas.
gas-evm-step-stop: STOP ends the run: {used} gas used, {left} gas left to return.
gas-evm-step-out-of-gas: SSTORE needs {cost} gas but only {left} is left, so the call runs out of gas: all {limit} gas is consumed and the write is reverted.
gas-evm-definition-deck: The plate everything stands on: the state of every account. Of the parts shown, only storage persists after the call.
gas-evm-definition-tank: The gas supply: the gas limit reserved for the transaction. Intrinsic gas and every opcode draw from it.
gas-evm-definition-evm: The Ethereum Virtual Machine. Its program counter steps through the contract's code, one opcode at a time.
gas-evm-definition-stack: Short-lived working values. Pushing one costs {cost} gas.
gas-evm-definition-memory: Scratch space for the call, cleared when it ends. Cheap, but growing it costs a little extra.
gas-evm-definition-storage: The contract's persistent state. Writing a new slot costs {cost} gas, far more than anything else here.
tx-apply-caption: Applying a transaction: a signed transaction moves the world state from t to t+1. The sender sends the recipient {value} and pays a fee, which is split between a burn and a tip to the validator.
tx-apply-description: The world state is a plate with two accounts on it, the sender's and the recipient's, joined by a pipe for the value, with a validator and a burn mark in front. Step {step1}: the sender signs a transaction sending the recipient {value} and submits it. Step {step2}: {value} flows from the sender's account to the recipient's. Step {step3}: the {fee} fee leaves the sender's account on a separate pipe and splits: the {burned} base fee is burned, and the {tip} tip goes on to the validator. Step {step4}: the sender's nonce goes up by one, and the world state becomes t+1: the sender has {sent} less, the recipient has {value} more.
tx-apply-step-idle: Apply the transaction to follow how it changes the world state, step by step.
tx-apply-step-submit: Step {step}: the sender signs a transaction sending the recipient {value} and submits it.
tx-apply-step-value: Step {step}: {value} flows from the sender's account to the recipient's.
tx-apply-step-fee: Step {step}: the {fee} fee splits: the {burned} base fee is burned and the {tip} tip goes to the validator.
tx-apply-step-commit: Step {step}: the sender's nonce goes up by one, and the world state becomes t+1: the sender has {sent} less, the recipient has {value} more.
tx-apply-definition-deck: Every account's balance and nonce. Each valid transaction moves it from one state to the next.
tx-apply-definition-sender: The externally owned account that sends the transaction. It pays the value and the fee, and its nonce counts its transactions.
tx-apply-definition-recipient: The account that receives the value.
tx-apply-definition-slip: The signed transaction: recipient, value, gas limit, fees and the sender's nonce.
tx-apply-definition-pipe: Carries the value from the sender to the recipient.
tx-apply-definition-burn: The base fee, gas used × base fee, is burned: removed from circulation for good.
tx-apply-definition-validator: The validator that included the transaction. It keeps the tip: gas used × priority fee.
tx-apply-definition-fee: The transaction fee, gas used × (base fee + priority fee). It splits into the burn and the tip.
evm-zones-caption: What survives a call: the EVM's parts sit in three zones. Machine state is cleared when the call ends, the code never changes, and only writes to storage remain.
evm-zones-description: A plate (world state) carries the EVM on a plinth (machine state) and, apart from it, the account's storage. The plinth holds the gas supply, the stack and memory; the EVM's code is a strip on its front, with the program counter as the lit cell. Step {step1}: the code is loaded, and it is immutable. Step {step2}: the call runs: values go on the stack, a word is written to memory, and gas drains. Step {step3}: SSTORE writes a value to a storage slot. Step {step4}: the call ends: the stack, memory and remaining gas are cleared, the code is unchanged, and the storage write remains.
evm-zones-step-idle: Run the call to see which parts of the EVM keep their contents when it ends.
evm-zones-step-load: Step {step}: the contract's code is loaded into the EVM. Code is immutable: no call can change it.
evm-zones-step-run: Step {step}: the call runs. The program counter steps through the code, values go on the stack, memory fills and gas drains.
evm-zones-step-store: Step {step}: SSTORE writes a value to a storage slot in the account's storage, part of the world state.
evm-zones-step-end: Step {step}: the call ends. Machine state is cleared, the code is unchanged, and the storage write remains.
evm-zones-storage-written: {count, plural, one {{slots} slot written} other {{slots} slots written}}
evm-zones-definition-deck: The state of every account, kept from block to block.
evm-zones-definition-machine: The program counter, stack, memory and gas supply: the EVM's working state during one call.
evm-zones-definition-evm: The contract's bytecode. The program counter steps through it one opcode at a time.
evm-zones-definition-tank: The gas supply left for this call. What remains at the end is returned.
evm-zones-definition-stack: Short-lived working values, up to {depth} deep.
evm-zones-definition-memory: Scratch space for the call, cleared when it ends.
evm-zones-definition-storage: The contract's own key-value store. Writes made here outlast the call, unless it reverts.
gas-tx-status-idle: Ready: choose a scenario and send it
gas-evm-status-idle: Ready: choose a scenario and run it
gas-evm-status-out-of-gas: Out of gas at SSTORE: write reverted
tx-apply-status-idle: World state t: ready to apply
evm-zones-status-run: Call running: stack, memory and gas in use
evm-zones-status-end: Call ended: only the storage write remains
accounts-caption: An account examined: its address leads to the account state, four fields. The nonce and balance are values; storageRoot and codeHash are hashes of the account's storage and its EVM code.
accounts-description: A plate (the account) carries, from left to right, the address, the account state as a stack of four slabs (nonce, balance, storageRoot and codeHash), and the two parts the hash slabs connect to: the account storage, a tank at the back, and the EVM code, a block at the front. Step {step1}: the address leads into the account state. Step {step2}: the nonce and the balance, in wei. Step {step3}: storageRoot, the root hash of the trie that encodes the account's storage. Step {step4}: codeHash, the hash of the account's EVM code. In the externally owned account scenario the storage tank is empty and the code block is an empty outline: its storage trie is empty, and its codeHash is the hash of an empty string.
accounts-step-idle: Choose a scenario and examine the account to follow its address and four fields, step by step.
accounts-step-address-eoa: Step {step}: every account has an address, which leads to its state. An externally owned account's address comes from its public key.
accounts-step-address-contract: Step {step}: every account has an address, which leads to its state. A contract account has no private key: its code controls it.
accounts-step-state-eoa: Step {step}: the account state starts with the nonce, {nonce}, the number of transactions this account has sent, and the balance: {wei} wei ({eth} ETH).
accounts-step-state-contract: Step {step}: the account state starts with the nonce, {nonce}, which is one more than the number of contracts this account has created (a contract's nonce starts at {start}), and the balance: {wei} wei ({eth} ETH).
accounts-step-storage-eoa: Step {step}: storageRoot is the root hash of the trie that encodes the account's storage. This account's storage is empty, the default, so it is the root of an empty trie.
accounts-step-storage-contract: Step {step}: storageRoot is a {bits}-bit hash of the root of the trie that encodes the account's storage, a mapping between {bits}-bit values.
accounts-step-code-eoa: Step {step}: this externally owned account has no code, so its codeHash is the hash of an empty string.
accounts-step-code-contract: Step {step}: codeHash is the hash of the account's EVM code, which runs when the account gets a message call. Unlike the other fields, it can't be changed.
accounts-status-storage-eoa: storageRoot: root of an empty trie
accounts-status-storage-contract: storageRoot: root of the storage trie
accounts-status-code-eoa: codeHash: hash of an empty string
accounts-status-code-contract: codeHash: hash of the EVM code
accounts-definition-deck: An entity with an ETH balance that can send messages on Ethereum: user-controlled, or a smart contract.
accounts-definition-address: The account's identifier: {bytes} bytes, written as 0x and {chars} hexadecimal characters.
accounts-definition-state: The account's four fields: nonce, balance, storageRoot and codeHash.
accounts-definition-storageRoot: A {bits}-bit hash of the root node of the Merkle Patricia Trie that encodes the account's storage.
accounts-definition-codeHash: The hash of the account's EVM code, under which the code is kept in the state database.
accounts-definition-storage: The account's storage: a mapping between {bits}-bit integer values, empty by default.
accounts-definition-code: Code that runs when the account gets a message call. A contract's code can't be changed. An externally owned account has none unless it delegates to a contract (EIP-7702).
block-state-caption: Applying a block: its transactions change the world state one at a time, in block order, each starting from the state the one before it left. Together they move the world state from t to t+1.
block-state-description: The world state is a plate with three accounts in a row: Alice, Bob and a contract, joined by pipes for value. Behind it stands the block: three transactions stacked in block order, the first on top. At the start, Alice has {aliceStart}, Bob has {bobStart} and the contract has {contractStart}. Step {step1}: transaction {tx1} applies first: Alice sends Bob {t1Value} and pays a {t1Fee} fee. Step {step2}: transaction {tx2} starts from the state transaction {tx1} left: Bob calls the contract with {t2Value}, which he can only cover because of transaction {tx1}. If the call succeeds, the contract keeps the {t2Value} and Bob pays a {t2Fee} fee. If the contract reverts the call, the {t2Value} transfer is undone, but Bob still pays a {t2RevertFee} fee, his nonce still goes up, and the transaction stays in the block. Step {step3}: transaction {tx3} starts from the state transaction {tx2} left: Bob sends Alice {t3Value} and pays a {t3Fee} fee. Step {step4}: with every transaction applied in order, the result is world state t+1. Each fee is split between a burn and a tip to the validator.
block-state-step-idle: Choose a scenario and apply the block to follow how its transactions change the world state, one at a time.
block-state-step-tx1: Step {step}: transaction {tx1} applies first. Alice sends Bob {t1Value} and pays a {t1Fee} fee.
block-state-step-tx2: Step {step}: transaction {tx2} starts from the state transaction {tx1} left, so Bob can now cover sending the contract {t2Value}. He pays a {t2Fee} fee.
block-state-step-tx2-revert: Step {step}: transaction {tx2} calls the contract, which reverts. The {t2Value} transfer is undone, but Bob still pays a {t2Fee} fee and his nonce still goes up.
block-state-step-tx3: Step {step}: transaction {tx3} starts from the state transaction {tx2} left. Bob sends Alice {t3Value} and pays a {t3Fee} fee.
block-state-step-seal: Step {step}: every transaction is applied, in block order, and the result is world state t+1. Any node that re-executes the block arrives at the same state.
block-state-status-idle: World state t: block ready to apply
block-state-status-seal: World state t+1 · Bob's nonce change {nonce}
block-state-definition-deck: Every account's state: balance, nonce, code and storage. A block's transactions, applied in order, move it from one state to the next. This example tracks balances and nonces.
block-state-definition-block: An ordered list of transactions, applied first to last. A reverted transaction stays in the block.
block-state-definition-alice: Alice's externally owned account. It sends the first transaction.
block-state-definition-bob: Bob's externally owned account. It sends the second and third transactions; its nonce counts them.
block-state-definition-contract: A contract account. Its code runs when Bob calls it, and can revert the call.
node-clients-definition-deck: One computer running both clients. Together they verify blocks and keep track of the head of the chain.
node-clients-definition-cl: Runs proof-of-stake consensus: receives blocks from peers, runs fork choice and keeps track of the head of the chain.
node-clients-definition-el: Executes transactions in the EVM and holds Ethereum's state and transaction pool.
node-clients-definition-engine: The local RPC connection the consensus client uses to drive the execution client.
node-clients-definition-app: Software that uses the node, such as a wallet or a library like ethers.js or viem.
node-clients-definition-rpc: The execution client's API for users. Its eth_ methods query the chain and submit transactions.
node-clients-definition-beacon: The consensus client's HTTP API, for its status and consensus data such as blocks.
node-clients-definition-cl-net: Other nodes' consensus clients. They gossip blocks and attestations.
node-clients-definition-el-net: Other nodes' execution clients. They gossip transactions.
node-clients-definition-mempool: Transactions this node has received and checked, waiting to be included in a block.
node-clients-definition-evm: The execution client's built-in computer, which executes the transactions in each block.
node-clients-definition-validator: Holds a staker's validator keys. It gets its duties from the consensus client over the Beacon API and signs blocks and attestations.
node-clients-caption: A node runs two clients. Apps call the execution client over JSON-RPC and the consensus client over the Beacon API, and the consensus client drives the execution client over the Engine API.
node-clients-description: A plate (the node) carries a consensus client and an execution client, joined by the Engine API. Each client is linked to its own group of peers off the plate. In front, a wallet or app has one pipe to each client. Step {step1}: the app calls the execution client's JSON-RPC API, for example eth_blockNumber. Step {step2}: the app calls the consensus client's Beacon API, for example to check whether it is synced. Step {step3}: the consensus client drives the execution client over the Engine API, while each client gossips with its own peers.
node-clients-step-idle: Send the requests to see which client answers each API, and how the two clients work together.
node-clients-step-rpc: Step {step}: a wallet or app calls the execution client's JSON-RPC API. Methods in the eth_ namespace query the chain and submit transactions.
node-clients-step-beacon: Step {step}: the app calls the consensus client's Beacon API, an HTTP API for the client's status and consensus data such as blocks.
node-clients-step-engine: Step {step}: the consensus client drives the execution client over the Engine API, a local RPC connection. Each client also gossips with its own peer-to-peer network.
node-clients-status-rpc: JSON-RPC: answered by the execution client
node-clients-status-beacon: Beacon API: answered by the consensus client
node-clients-status-engine: Engine API: consensus client to execution client
node-clients-architecture-caption: Each client has its own peer-to-peer network: consensus clients gossip blocks, execution clients gossip transactions. The Engine API joins the two clients.
node-clients-architecture-description: A plate (the node) carries a consensus client, with a short chain of blocks on top, and an execution client, with its transaction pool and the EVM on top. The Engine API arches between them. Behind the node, consensus peers; in front of it, execution peers, each group on its own link. In front of the node, a wallet or app is linked to both clients. Scenario new block: step {step1}, a block arrives from a consensus peer and the consensus client checks it; step {step2}, the consensus client sends the block's execution payload to the execution client with engine_newPayload; step {step3}, the execution client executes the transactions in the EVM, checks the result against the block header and replies VALID; step {step4}, the consensus client runs fork choice, makes the block the head of its chain and calls engine_forkchoiceUpdated. Scenario new transaction: step {step1}, a transaction arrives from an execution peer; step {step2}, the execution client checks it and adds it to its transaction pool; step {step3}, it passes the transaction on to its other peers.
node-clients-architecture-step-idle: Choose a scenario, then receive the block or transaction to follow it through the node.
node-clients-architecture-step-gossip: Step {step}: a new block arrives from a peer on the consensus client's peer-to-peer network. The consensus client checks that it came from a valid sender with correct metadata.
node-clients-architecture-step-payload: Step {step}: the consensus client sends the block's execution payload, its transactions and related data, to the execution client with engine_newPayload.
node-clients-architecture-step-execute: Step {step}: the execution client executes the transactions in the EVM, checks that the result matches the block header, and replies VALID.
node-clients-architecture-step-forkchoic: Step {step}: the consensus client runs fork choice and makes the block the head of its chain, then calls engine_forkchoiceUpdated so the execution client follows the same head.
node-clients-architecture-step-arrive: Step {step}: a new transaction arrives from a peer on the execution client's peer-to-peer network.
node-clients-architecture-step-pool: Step {step}: the execution client checks the transaction and adds it to its transaction pool, where it waits to be included in a block.
node-clients-architecture-step-regossip: Step {step}: the execution client passes the transaction on to its other peers, so it spreads across the network.
node-clients-architecture-status-payload: Execution payload sent over the Engine API
node-clients-architecture-status-forkcho: Fork choice: the block is the new head
node-clients-architecture-status-pool: Checked and added to the pool
node-clients-access-title: Using Ethereum through your own node
node-clients-access-caption: A wallet connected to your own node gets its answers from data your node has verified, and sends transactions straight to the network, with no provider in between.
node-clients-access-description: A plate (the node) carries a consensus client, with a short chain of blocks on top, and an execution client, with its transaction pool and the EVM on top, joined by the Engine API. Consensus peers sit behind the node and execution peers in front of it. In front of the node, a wallet or app is linked to both clients. Step {step1}: the wallet asks the execution client for an account's balance with eth_getBalance. Step {step2}: the execution client answers from the state your node has verified itself, so no one else learns which address was asked about. Step {step3}: the wallet submits a signed transaction with eth_sendRawTransaction, and the execution client checks it and adds it to its transaction pool. Step {step4}: the execution client passes the transaction on to its peers. Step {step5}: a block arrives from a consensus peer, and the node verifies it itself: the consensus client checks it and the execution client executes it.
node-clients-access-step-idle: Use your node to follow a wallet's requests through it, from a balance query to the block that includes a transaction.
node-clients-access-step-query: Step {step}: your wallet asks your node's execution client for an account's balance over JSON-RPC, with eth_getBalance.
node-clients-access-step-answer: Step {step}: the execution client answers from the state your node has verified itself. No provider sees which addresses you ask about.
node-clients-access-step-send: Step {step}: the wallet submits a signed transaction with eth_sendRawTransaction. The execution client checks it and adds it to its transaction pool.
node-clients-access-step-gossip: Step {step}: the execution client passes the transaction on to its peers, and from them it spreads across the network.
node-clients-access-step-verify: Step {step}: a block arrives from a consensus peer. Your node checks it against the consensus rules itself: the consensus client checks the block and the execution client executes it.
node-clients-access-status-answer: Answered from your node's own state
node-clients-access-status-send: Transaction checked and added to the pool
node-clients-setup-caption: A node runs an execution client and a consensus client, connected over the authenticated Engine API. A validator client is optional, for staking.
node-clients-setup-description: A plate (the node) carries a consensus client and an execution client. The Engine API arches between them, with a lock on it for the shared JWT secret. Each client is linked to its own group of peers off the plate. A validator client stands off the plate's front-left corner, linked to the consensus client, and a wallet or app in front of the node is linked to both clients. Step {step1}: the consensus client connects to the execution client's Engine API, on port {engine} by default, authenticated with a JWT secret file both clients are given. Step {step2}: each client connects to its own peers and syncs; the execution client listens on port {peers}, TCP and UDP. Step {step3}: if you stake, a validator client connects to the consensus client's Beacon API. Step {step4}: wallets and apps call the execution client's JSON-RPC API, on port {rpc}, which by default is reachable only from the same computer.
node-clients-setup-step-idle: Connect the clients to see each connection a node needs, and its default port.
node-clients-setup-step-engine: Step {step}: the consensus client connects to the execution client's Engine API, on port {engine} by default. Both clients are given the path to the same JWT secret file, which authenticates the connection.
node-clients-setup-step-peers: Step {step}: each client connects to its own peers and syncs the chain. The execution client listens on port {peers}, TCP and UDP, which should be open in your router and firewall.
node-clients-setup-step-validator: Step {step}: if you stake, a validator client connects to the consensus client's Beacon API. It holds the validator keys and signs blocks and attestations.
node-clients-setup-step-rpc: Step {step}: wallets and apps call the execution client's JSON-RPC API, on port {rpc}. By default it is reachable only from the same computer.
node-clients-networks-caption: Consensus clients gossip blocks and attestations on one peer-to-peer network, execution clients gossip transactions on another, and the Engine API joins the two clients inside the node.
node-clients-networks-description: A plate (the node) carries a consensus client, with a short chain of blocks on top, and an execution client, with its transaction pool and the EVM on top, joined by the Engine API, a local RPC connection. Consensus peers sit behind the node, on the consensus peer-to-peer network (libp2p), and execution peers in front of it, on the execution peer-to-peer network (devp2p). Scenario receive a block: step {step1}, a block arrives over consensus gossip and the consensus client pre-validates it; step {step2}, the consensus client sends its execution payload to the execution client with engine_newPayload; step {step3}, the execution client executes it, checks the result against the block header and replies VALID; step {step4}, the consensus client makes the block the head of its chain and, if one of its validators is due to attest, gossips an attestation for it. Scenario propose a block: step {step1}, transactions arrive over execution gossip and wait in the transaction pool; step {step2}, the consensus client calls engine_forkchoiceUpdated with payload attributes and the execution client starts building a payload from its pool; step {step3}, the consensus client calls engine_getPayload and puts the returned payload into a new beacon block; step {step4}, the signed block is gossiped to consensus peers.
node-clients-networks-step-idle: Choose a scenario, then run it to see which network carries each step.
node-clients-networks-step-gossip: Step {step}: a block arrives over the consensus peer-to-peer network. The consensus client pre-validates it: it came from a valid sender, with correct metadata.
node-clients-networks-step-payload: Step {step}: over the Engine API, a local RPC connection, the consensus client sends the block's execution payload to the execution client with engine_newPayload.
node-clients-networks-step-valid: Step {step}: the execution client executes the transactions, checks that the result matches the block header, and replies VALID over the Engine API.
node-clients-networks-step-attest: Step {step}: the consensus client makes the block the head of its chain. If one of its validators is due to attest, it gossips an attestation over the consensus peer-to-peer network.
node-clients-networks-step-fill: Step {step}: transactions arrive over the execution peer-to-peer network and wait in the execution client's transaction pool.
node-clients-networks-step-build: Step {step}: one of the node's validators is due to propose. The consensus client calls engine_forkchoiceUpdated with payload attributes, and the execution client starts building a payload from its pool.
node-clients-networks-step-get: Step {step}: the consensus client calls engine_getPayload. The execution client returns the payload, and the consensus client puts it into a new beacon block.
node-clients-networks-step-broadcast: Step {step}: the validator signs the block, and the consensus client gossips it over the consensus peer-to-peer network. Other nodes check it as in the receive scenario.
node-clients-networks-status-payload: Payload sent over the Engine API
node-clients-networks-status-get: Payload returned to the consensus client
attestations-caption: The attestation lifecycle: validators sign attestations, aggregators combine each committee's attestations into one aggregate, and a block proposer merges the aggregates into one attestation in its block.
attestations-description: One plate carries the attestation lifecycle, with messages moving from the back to the front. At the back stand two committees, A and B, of {members} validators each. In each, the last member, a taller block, is also the committee's aggregator; one validator in committee B is offline. Each committee's validators are joined to their aggregator by their subnet. The aggregators connect to a block of beacon nodes, which connects to the block proposer. Along the front runs the beacon chain: its head block, then empty slots for the next blocks. Step {step1}: each online validator signs an attestation. Step {step2}: the attestations are gossiped on each committee's subnet to its aggregator. Step {step3}: each aggregator combines the matching attestations into one aggregate, whose aggregation bits mark who signed: {signedA} of {members} in committee A, {signedB} of {members} in committee B. Step {step4}: the aggregates are broadcast to the beacon nodes, which gossip them on to the proposer. Step {step5}: the two aggregates share the same data, so the proposer merges them into one attestation in the block for the next slot. If that slot's proposer is missing, the slot stays empty and the following proposer includes it instead.
attestations-step-idle: Choose a scenario and attest to follow two committees' attestations from signing to inclusion in a block.
attestations-step-generate: Step {step}: generation. Each validator in the two committees builds its attestation data, its vote for the head block and the source and target checkpoints, then signs it. A validator in committee B is offline and doesn't attest.
attestations-step-propagate: Step {step}: propagation. Each attestation is gossiped on its committee's subnet, where the committee's aggregator hears it.
attestations-step-aggregate: Step {step}: aggregation. Each aggregator combines the attestations whose data matches its own into one aggregate with a single signature. Its aggregation bits record each sender: committee B's offline validator leaves a {zero}.
attestations-step-broadcast: Step {step}: propagation of the aggregate. The aggregators broadcast their aggregates to the wider network, and the beacon nodes gossip them on to every node, the block proposer's included.
attestations-step-include: Step {step}: inclusion. The two aggregates carry the same data, so the proposer of the next slot merges them into one attestation in its block: its committee bits mark committees A and B, and its aggregation bits record who signed in each. Inclusion delay: {delay}.
attestations-step-include-missed: Step {step}: inclusion. The proposer of the next slot is missing, so that slot stays empty. The following proposer merges the two aggregates into one attestation in its block instead, an inclusion delay of {delay}, so these validators lose the head reward.
attestations-status-broadcast: Aggregates gossiped to every beacon node
attestations-status-include: Merged into one attestation in the next block
attestations-status-include-missed: Slot missed: included a slot later
attestations-definition-validators: Validators assigned to a committee for this slot. Each signs one attestation: its vote for the head block and the source and target checkpoints.
attestations-definition-aggregator: A committee member selected for the slot to collect matching attestations from its subnet and combine them into one aggregate.
attestations-definition-network: The peer-to-peer network of beacon nodes. It gossips aggregates to every node, so the next block proposer hears them.
attestations-definition-proposer: The validator chosen to propose the next block. It packs the aggregates it has heard into that block, merging those with the same data into one attestation.
attestations-definition-block: The block that includes the attestation. Aggregates with the same data from different committees are merged into one, whose committee bits show which committees it covers.
attestations-definition-chain: The beacon chain. The attestations vote for its latest block as the head of the chain.
attestations-definition-subnet: Gossip subnets. A committee's attestations travel on one of {count} attestation subnets, not across the whole network.
validator-keys-caption: A wallet funds validators. Each validator signs with its own signing key, separate from the wallet's key, and pays out to a withdrawal address.
validator-keys-description: One plate carries the staker's wallet at the back left, the deposit contract in the middle and the validators along the front. Each validator carries its signing key, a cube; with {from} credentials each also has a withdrawal key, a flat slab on the plate in front of it, joined to it by a short pipe. Once a withdrawal address is set, it appears as its own block along the back of the plate, linked to the validators: it can be the wallet that made the deposits or any other address. With {from} or {address} credentials the wallet stakes {stake} ETH as {three} validators of {amount} ETH each; with {compounding} it stakes the same {stake} ETH in one validator, since one {compounding} validator can hold up to {max} ETH. Step {step1}: the wallet sends one deposit per validator to the deposit contract. Each carries deposit data: one validator's public signing key and its withdrawal credentials. Step {step2}: the beacon chain processes the deposits and activates the validators, each identified by its public signing key. Step {step3}: each validator signs blocks and attestations with its signing private key. Step {step4} depends on the withdrawal credentials. With {from}, no withdrawal address is set until the withdrawal key signs a BLSToExecutionChange message for the beacon chain pointing the validator at an execution address, which changes its credentials to {to}. With {address}, the validators have no BLS withdrawal key, the balance above {amount} ETH is swept to the withdrawal address automatically, and the withdrawal address's key can request their exit. With {compounding}, rewards compound in the validator's balance, a block that grows on top of it, up to {max} ETH, only the balance above that is swept, and the withdrawal address's key requests exits and partial withdrawals.
validator-keys-step-idle: Choose a scenario and deposit to follow one wallet staking {stake} ETH, with keys for each validator.
validator-keys-step-deposit: Step {step}: deposit. The wallet sends {n, plural, one {{count} deposit} other {{count} deposits}} of {amount} ETH each to the deposit contract. Each carries deposit data: one validator's public signing key and its withdrawal credentials, {prefix}.
validator-keys-step-deposit-compounding: Step {step}: deposit. One {prefix} validator can hold up to {max} ETH, so the wallet sends a single deposit of {amount} ETH instead of splitting it across validators. The deposit data carries the validator's public signing key and its withdrawal credentials, {prefix}.
validator-keys-step-activate: Step {step}: activation. {n, plural, one {The beacon chain processes the deposit and activates {count} validator, identified by the public signing key in its deposit data.} other {The beacon chain processes the deposits and activates {count} validators, each identified by the public signing key in its deposit data.}}
validator-keys-step-sign: Step {step}: signing. {n, plural, one {The validator signs blocks and attestations with its signing private key, kept online.} other {Each validator signs blocks and attestations with its own signing private key, kept online.}} The wallet's key plays no part.
validator-keys-step-withdraw-bls: Step {step}: withdrawal credentials. With {from} credentials no withdrawal address is set, so no ETH can leave. Each withdrawal key signs a BLSToExecutionChange message for the beacon chain, pointing its validator at an execution address and changing its credentials to {to}.
validator-keys-step-withdraw-address: Step {step}: withdrawals. The deposit data set {prefix} credentials pointing at a withdrawal address, here a separate one from the wallet, so the balance above {amount} ETH is swept there automatically. These validators have no BLS withdrawal key: the withdrawal address's key can also request their exit.
validator-keys-step-withdraw-compounding: Step {step}: compounding. With {prefix} credentials, rewards compound in the validator's balance up to {max} ETH; only the excess is swept to the withdrawal address. There is no BLS withdrawal key: the withdrawal address's key requests exits and partial withdrawals.
validator-keys-status-deposit: {n, plural, one {{count} deposit} other {{count} deposits}} sent
validator-keys-status-activate: {n, plural, one {{count} validator active} other {{count} validators active}}
validator-keys-status-sign: Each validator signs with its own key
validator-keys-status-withdraw-address: Excess balance swept to the withdrawal address
validator-keys-definition-wallet: The staker's wallet: an account with its own key, separate from the validator keys. It pays for the deposits.
validator-keys-definition-mnemonic: A list of words, the one secret behind every key here. It becomes a seed, and the seed becomes the master key, m.
validator-keys-definition-contract: The staking deposit contract. The beacon chain reads each deposit made to it and adds a validator for it.
validator-keys-definition-paths: Branches of the key tree. A path such as {signingPath} leads from the master key m to one key; the index i picks the validator.
validator-keys-definition-validators: Validators run by one staker. Each is identified by its public signing key.
validator-keys-definition-signing: A BLS key pair, one per validator (the page's 'validator key'). The private key signs blocks and attestations, so it stays online; the public key identifies the validator.
validator-keys-definition-withdrawal: A BLS key pair, one per validator with {bls} credentials, kept offline. It's needed only to change those credentials to an execution address.
validator-keys-definition-payout: The execution address the withdrawal credentials point to. Withdrawals are paid there, and its key can request exits. It can be the wallet that made the deposits or any other address, such as one kept in cold storage.
validator-keys-definition-master: The master key m, made from the mnemonic's seed: the root every derivation path starts from.
validator-keys-definition-balance: The validator's balance. With {compounding} credentials its rewards stay in it and compound.
validator-keys-derive-caption: Keys from one mnemonic: each validator gets a withdrawal key and, one level below it, a signing key.
validator-keys-derive-description: One plate carries a mnemonic at the back and {count} validators along the front, each with a flat slab on the plate in front of it for its withdrawal key. Step {step1}: the mnemonic becomes a seed, and the seed the master key m, a small block where the paths branch. Step {step2}: following the path {withdrawalPath}, where i is each validator's index, derives one withdrawal key per validator, along a path from m to each slab. Step {step3}: one level further down, {signingPath} derives each validator's signing key from its withdrawal key's branch: a short pipe joins each slab to the cube on its validator. Step {step4}: each public signing key goes into one validator's deposit data; another validator would take the next index, so the one mnemonic backs up every key.
validator-keys-derive-step-idle: Derive keys to follow one mnemonic generating the withdrawal and signing keys of {count} validators.
validator-keys-derive-step-seed: Step {step}: master key. The mnemonic is turned into a seed, and the seed into the master key m: the root of a tree of keys.
validator-keys-derive-step-withdrawal: Step {step}: withdrawal keys. Each validator has its own index i in the path {withdrawalPath}, so the same master key derives one withdrawal key per validator: {count} here.
validator-keys-derive-step-signing: Step {step}: signing keys. One level further down, {signingPath} derives each validator's signing key from its branch. Knowing a signing key doesn't reveal the withdrawal key above it.
validator-keys-derive-step-validators: Step {step}: validators. Each public signing key goes into one validator's deposit data. Another validator takes the next index, so writing down the one mnemonic backs up every key.
ex-ante-reorg-caption: A one-block ex-ante reorg: the attacker withholds block B and its votes, then releases them as honest block C appears, so the next block builds on B and C is orphaned. Proposer boost defeats an attacker this small.
ex-ante-reorg-description: One plate carries slots {n} to {n3}, from back-left to front-right, named along its front edge. The back lane is the chain honest validators see: block A in slot {n}, an empty slot {n1}, then block C in slot {n2}. The front lane is the attacker's branch: block B in slot {n1}, built on A, fed by the attacker's validators in the front-left corner. Each lane runs on into a tank of the votes behind that branch, both fed by the committee at the front-right end. Every slot's committee is drawn as {committee} equal votes, {attacker} of them the attacker's. Step {step1}: the attacker proposes B and attests to it with its {attacker} votes, but publishes neither, so B's tank shows them only as a dashed ghost level; the other {honest} see an empty slot and vote for A. Step {step2}: an honest proposer publishes C on A. Step {step3}: the attacker releases B and its {attacker} votes at almost the same moment. Step {step4}: the slot {n2} committee votes. Step {step5}: the honest proposer of slot {n3} builds block D on the heavier branch. Before proposer boost, honest validators see B ahead and vote for it, so D builds on B and C is orphaned. With proposer boost, C arrives on time and gets weight equal to {boost} votes, more than B's {attacker}, so honest validators vote for C, D builds on C and B is orphaned. An attacker with more than a third of each committee would still win, because its votes from both slots would outweigh the honest votes for C once the boost ends.
ex-ante-reorg-step-idle: Choose a scenario and attack to follow a one-block ex-ante reorg, slot by slot.
ex-ante-reorg-step-withhold: Step {step}: slot {n1}. The attacker proposes block B on A, and its {attacker} validators in the slot's committee vote for B, but it publishes neither. The other {honest} see an empty slot and vote for A as the head.
ex-ante-reorg-step-propose-no-boost: Step {step}: slot {n2}. An honest proposer publishes block C on A, the head it sees.
ex-ante-reorg-step-propose-boost: Step {step}: slot {n2}. An honest proposer publishes block C on A, the head it sees. C arrives on time, so fork choice gives it proposer boost: weight equal to {boost} votes, until the slot ends.
ex-ante-reorg-step-release-no-boost: Step {step}: almost as C appears, the attacker releases block B and its {attacker} withheld votes. B now has {votesB} votes and C {votesC}, so B is the head.
ex-ante-reorg-step-release-boost: Step {step}: almost as C appears, the attacker releases block B and its {attacker} withheld votes. B's {votesB} votes are fewer than C's boost of {boost}, so C stays the head.
ex-ante-reorg-step-vote-no-boost: Step {step}: the slot {n2} committee votes. Honest validators see B ahead and vote for it, with the attacker. B's branch has {votesB} votes, C's {votesC}.
ex-ante-reorg-step-vote-boost: Step {step}: the slot {n2} committee votes. The {honest} honest validators see C ahead and vote for it; only the attacker's {attacker} vote for B. C's branch has {votesC} votes, B's {votesB}.
ex-ante-reorg-step-build-no-boost: Step {step}: slot {n3}. The honest proposer builds block D on B, the heavier branch. C is orphaned: the attacker has reorged an honest block out of the chain.
ex-ante-reorg-step-build-boost: Step {step}: slot {n3}. The boost has ended, but C's branch still leads, so block D builds on C. B is orphaned and the attack fails: the attacker's {votesB} votes from both slots fall short of C's {votesC}. An attacker with more than a third of each committee would still win.
ex-ante-reorg-status-propose-boost: Block C published, with proposer boost
ex-ante-reorg-status-release-no-boost: B released: B is the head
ex-ante-reorg-status-release-boost: B released: C keeps the head
ex-ante-reorg-status-build-no-boost: D builds on B: C orphaned
ex-ante-reorg-status-build-boost: D builds on C: B orphaned
ex-ante-reorg-definition-a: The block in slot {n}, the last block every validator has seen. Both branches build on it.
ex-ante-reorg-definition-empty: Slot {n1} as honest validators see it: no block arrived, so they vote for A as the head.
ex-ante-reorg-definition-b: The attacker's block for slot {n1}, built on A and kept hidden until slot {n2}.
ex-ante-reorg-definition-c: The honest block for slot {n2}. Its proposer never saw B, so it builds on A.
ex-ante-reorg-definition-d: The honest block for slot {n3}. Its proposer builds on whichever branch fork choice finds heavier.
ex-ante-reorg-definition-attacker: Validators run by the attacker: {attacker} of every committee's {committee} votes here, and the proposer of slot {n1}.
ex-ante-reorg-definition-weight: Votes behind each branch. Fork choice follows the heavier branch.
ex-ante-reorg-definition-boost: Extra weight for a block that arrives on time, equal to {boost} of a committee's {committee} votes, until its slot ends.
ex-ante-reorg-definition-committee: One slot's committee: {committee} votes, {attacker} of them the attacker's. Its votes go to the branch each member sees as the head.
mev-boost-definition-node: The validator's machine: its consensus, execution and validator clients, with MEV-Boost running beside them.
mev-boost-definition-proposer: The consensus client and validator client of the validator chosen to propose this slot's block.
mev-boost-definition-boost: Software beside the consensus client that asks each relay the proposer has chosen for its best bid, and passes on the highest.
mev-boost-definition-relays: Services that check builders' blocks and hold them until the proposer signs, then publish them. Builders and proposers both have to trust them.
mev-boost-definition-builders: Specialized parties that order transactions and searchers' bundles into the most valuable block they can, and bid for it to be proposed.
mev-boost-definition-network: Other nodes. They receive the published block over consensus gossip and verify it.
mev-boost-caption: With MEV-Boost, a proposer sells its block space: builders bid through relays, and the proposer signs the best block's header without seeing its transactions.
mev-boost-description: Across the front, from left to right: the proposer's node, with its consensus client and MEV-Boost beside it; a pad of relays; a pad of builders. Behind the node, a pad of peers stands for the rest of the network. Step {step1}: before its slot, the proposer registers with the relays through MEV-Boost, giving the fee recipient address and gas limit it wants. Step {step2}: builders build blocks from public transactions and searchers' bundles and send them to the relays with a bid, and the relays check each block. Step {step3}: in its slot, the proposer asks for a header; MEV-Boost asks every relay and passes on the highest bid, {bid} ETH, with its block's header but not its transactions. Step {step4}: the proposer signs a blinded block, which holds the header but no transactions, and sends it to the relay holding that bid. Step {step5}: the relay checks the signature and publishes the full block to the network. If no relay answers in time, the proposer builds a block with its own execution client instead.
mev-boost-step-idle: Propose a block to follow it from the builders' bids to the block the relay publishes.
mev-boost-step-register: Step {step}: before its slot, the proposer registers with its relays through MEV-Boost: the fee recipient address it wants paid, and its gas limit.
mev-boost-step-bid: Step {step}: builders build blocks from public transactions and searchers' bundles, and send them to the relays with a bid. The relays check each block before offering it.
mev-boost-step-header: Step {step}: in its slot, the proposer asks for a block header. MEV-Boost asks every relay and passes on the highest bid, with its block's header but not its transactions.
mev-boost-step-sign: Step {step}: the proposer signs a blinded block, holding the header but no transactions, and sends it to the relay with the winning bid. Signing commits it to that block.
mev-boost-step-publish: Step {step}: the relay checks the signature and publishes the full block to the network. The block pays the bid to the proposer's fee recipient.
mev-boost-status-bid: Builders' blocks and bids held by the relays
mev-boost-status-publish: Full block published by the relay
